# The Song of the First River

In the time before time, when the world was still learning its shape, there lived a mountain who wept stones instead of tears. The mountain was lonely, for nothing could grow on its harsh slopes, and no creature would make its home there.

One day, a cloud took pity on the mountain and asked, "Why do you weep stones when water would serve you better?"

The mountain replied, "I have forgotten the language of softness. I know only hardness and strength."

The cloud descended and wrapped herself around the mountain's peak. "Then I shall teach you," she whispered. Day after day, she shared her stories of the sky, of gentle rains and morning mists, of the joy found in yielding and flowing.

Slowly, the mountain's heart softened. Its stone tears began to melt, becoming the first drops of water. These drops joined together, trickling down the slopes, carving paths through ancient rock. The water sang as it flowed, and its song called forth seeds sleeping in the stone. Soon, grass and flowers followed the water's path.

Thus the first river was born—not from stone alone, but from the meeting of strength and gentleness, teaching us that the hardest hearts can learn to flow.

# The Weaver of Dawn

In the time before time, darkness covered the world like a heavy blanket. The people stumbled blindly, unable to see their loved ones or find their way home.

High in the mountains lived an old weaver named Alara, whose fingers moved with mysterious grace. One night, she dreamed of a golden thread that could push back the darkness. When she awoke, Alara climbed to the highest peak, where the sky touched the earth.

There, she found a single strand of starlight caught on a sharp rock. Carefully, she wound it around her spindle and began to weave. For seven days and seven nights, her loom clicked and clacked. With each pass of the shuttle, the fabric grew brighter, warmer, more radiant.

On the eighth morning, Alara lifted her creation—a tapestry of pure light—and hung it in the sky. The darkness fled, and warmth spread across the land. The people rejoiced, seeing each other clearly for the first time.

But Alara's work was not finished. Each evening, she takes down the tapestry to repair the threads worn thin by the day. Each morning, she hangs it anew.

This is why we have dawn—the weaver's daily gift to the world.
